gancho: Uma taça romana do século IV fica verde com luz pela frente e vermelha com luz por trás. O segredo são partículas de ouro e prata de uns 70 nanômetros, e os vidreiros talvez nem soubessem que havia ouro na mistura.
explicacao: A Taça de Licurgo, que o Museu Britânico comprou em 1958, é um copo de vidro romano entalhado com uma cena mitológica: o rei Licurgo preso por uma videira. O vidro é dicroico, ou seja, muda de cor conforme a luz o atravessa ou não. Estima-se que a massa tenha recebido cerca de 330 partes por milhão de prata e 40 de ouro, que formaram grãos de uma liga dos dois metais com uns 70 nanômetros, invisíveis ao microscópio comum: só um microscópio eletrônico os revela. Nesse tamanho, próximo ao comprimento de onda da luz visível, surge um efeito chamado ressonância de plásmon de superfície. Na luz que atravessa o vidro, as partículas espalham mais o azul que o vermelho, e o que chega ao olho é vermelho. Como os romanos chegaram a isso continua incerto. O mais provável é que tenha sido por acaso, com pó fino de ouro e prata contaminando a mistura; as quantidades são tão pequenas que os artesãos talvez nem soubessem do ouro. Só nos estudos de 1950 ficou certo que a taça era de vidro, e não de pedra preciosa. Em 2020, pesquisadores holandeses reproduziram o efeito verde e vermelho num material para impressão 3D, com nanopartículas de prata e ouro.

fontes.trecho: The Lycurgus Cup is a  Roman glass 4th-century cage cup made of a dichroic glass, which shows a different colour depending on whether or not light is passing through it: red when lit from behind and green when lit from in front. [...] showing the mythical King Lycurgus, who (depending on the version) tried to kill Ambrosia, a follower of the god Dionysus (Bacchus to the Romans). She was transformed into a vine that twined around the enraged king and restrained him [...] The dichroic effect is achieved by making the glass with tiny proportions of nanoparticles of gold and silver dispersed in colloidal form throughout the glass material. The process used remains unclear, and it is likely that it was not well understood or controlled by the makers, and was probably discovered by accidental "contamination" with minutely ground gold and silver dust. The glass-makers may not even have known that gold was involved, as the quantities involved are so tiny [...] It is estimated that to a conventionally composed Roman glass flux 330 parts per million of silver and 40 of gold were added: "These particles were precipitated as colloids and form a silver-gold alloy. [...] In transmitted light the fine particles scatter the blue end of the spectrum more effectively than the red end, resulting in red transmission, and this is the colour observed. [...] The particles are only about 70 nanometers across, and embedded in the glass, so they cannot be seen by optical microscopy, and a transmission electron microscope is needed instead. At this size they approach the size of the wavelengths of visible light, and a surface plasmon resonance effect takes place. [...] it was not until the first full studies of the cup in 1950 that it was established for certain that the material was glass and not a gemstone [...] In 1958, Victor, Lord Rothschild sold it to the British Museum for £20,000 [...] In 2020, researchers from the Netherlands reproduced the green/red dichroic effect in a 3D printable nanocomposite material. As with the original Lycurgus cup, this effect is due to small amounts of silver and gold nanoparticles

gancho: O arco-íris tem sete cores por escolha de Newton. Ele começou com cinco e depois acrescentou o laranja e o anil, para que as cores casassem com as sete notas da escala musical.
explicacao: Em meados da década de 1660, o jovem Isaac Newton comprou um par de prismas numa feira perto de Cambridge. Fez passar um feixe estreito de luz do Sol por um deles e obteve na parede uma faixa colorida como a de um arco-íris. Ele reconhecia que o espectro é contínuo, com uma variedade indefinida de tons intermediários, mas precisava dar nomes. Em 1672, dividiu-o em cinco cores principais: vermelho, amarelo, verde, azul e violeta. Mais tarde incluiu o laranja e o anil ("indigo"), chegando a sete por analogia com as notas de uma escala musical. A ideia vinha de uma crença dos antigos gregos, que ligavam as cores às notas, aos astros conhecidos do Sistema Solar e aos dias da semana. O próprio Newton admitiu que seus olhos não eram muito bons para distinguir cores. Na época, a Companhia das Índias Orientais começava a levar para a Inglaterra o corante índigo, que ia tomando o lugar do pastel-dos-tintureiros. Estudiosos observam que o "azul" de Newton seria o que hoje chamamos de ciano, e o seu "anil" seria o nosso azul, embora outros discordem. Hoje o arco-íris costuma ser dividido de outras formas, e a sensação de cores separadas é um efeito da percepção humana: o número de faixas é uma escolha um tanto arbitrária.

fontes.trecho: the most commonly cited and remembered sequence is Isaac Newton's sevenfold red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet [...] The apparent discreteness of main colours is an artefact of human perception and the exact number of main colours is a somewhat arbitrary choice. [...] Newton, who admitted his eyes were not very critical in distinguishing colours, originally (1672) divided the spectrum into five main colours: red, yellow, green, blue and violet. Later, he included orange and indigo, giving seven main colours by analogy to the number of notes in a musical scale. Newton chose to divide the visible spectrum into seven colours out of a belief derived from the beliefs of the ancient Greek sophists, who thought there was a connection between the colours, the musical notes, the known objects in the Solar System, and the days of the week. Scholars have noted that what Newton regarded at the time as "blue" would today be regarded as cyan, what Newton called "indigo" would today be called blue. [...] More modernly, the rainbow is often divided into

In the mid-1660s, when Newton bought a pair of prisms at a fair near Cambridge, the East India Company had begun importing indigo dye into England, supplanting the homegrown woad as source of blue dye. In a pivotal experiment in the history of optics, the young Newton shone a narrow beam of sunlight through a prism to produce a rainbow-like band of colors on the wall. In describing this optical spectrum, Newton acknowledged that the spectrum had a continuum of colors, but named seven: [...] Some later scientists have concluded that what Newton called "blue" was what is now called cyan or blue-green; and what Newton called "indigo" was what is now called blue. [...] However, other scholars reject this.

gancho: Platão e Euclides achavam que enxergamos porque os olhos lançam raios sobre as coisas. A ideia caiu há séculos, mas uma revisão de 2002 indicou que até metade dos universitários americanos ainda acredita em algo assim.
explicacao: A chamada teoria da emissão, ou extramissão, é antiga. No século V a.C., Empédocles dizia que Afrodite acendera um fogo dentro do olho, e esse fogo saía para iluminar o mundo. Platão a adotou por volta de 400 a.C., e Euclides, cerca de um século depois, estudou a geometria desses "raios visuais" em linha reta. No século II, o médico Galeno também a defendeu, e sua autoridade manteve a ideia viva entre médicos da Europa e do Oriente Médio. Os defensores citavam os olhos dos gatos, que brilham no escuro. Os críticos rebatiam: se fosse verdade, quem enxerga mal veria melhor quando alguém de vista boa olhasse para o mesmo objeto. Alhazen foi quem explicou que a visão acontece quando a luz refletida pelo objeto entra no olho, e a física do século XVII enterrou de vez a teoria antiga. Mesmo assim, uma revisão publicada em 2002 por psicólogos da Universidade Estadual de Ohio reuniu indícios de que até 50% dos universitários adultos nos Estados Unidos acreditam em algo saindo dos olhos durante a visão. Segundo os autores, as aulas tradicionais não bastavam para desfazer a crença, e havia alunos que saíam de cursos de psicologia sem entender direito como a visão funciona. Um estudo seguinte apontou uma possível origem: a sensação de que ver é algo que se dirige para fora.

fontes.trecho: Emission theory or extramission theory (variants: extromission) or extromissionism is the proposal that visual perception is accomplished by eye beams emitted by the eyes. [...] In the fifth century BC, Empedocles postulated that everything was composed of four elements; fire, air, earth, and water. He believed that Aphrodite made the human eye out of the four elements and that she lit the fire in the eye which shone out from the eye, making sight possible. [...] Around 400 BC, emission theory was held by Plato. Around 300 BC, Euclid wrote Optics and Catoptrics, in which he studied the properties of sight. Euclid postulated that the visual ray emitted from the eye travelled in straight lines [...] Galen, also in the 2nd century, likewise endorsed the extramission theory [...] his view held considerable influence in the pre-modern Middle East and Europe, especially among medical doctors in these regions. [...] The light from the eyes of some animals (such as cats, which modern science has determined have highly reflective eyes) could also be seen in "darkness". Adherents of intromission theory countered by saying that if emission theory were true, then someone with weak eyes should have their vision improved when someone with good eyes looks at the same objects. [...] Alhazen was the first person to explain that vision occurs when light reflects from an object into one's eyes. The rise of physics in the 17th century led to a novel version of the intromissionist theory that proved extremely influential and displaced any legacies of the old emissive theories. [...] Winer et al. (2002) have found evidence that as many as 50% of adult college students believe in emission theory.

fontes.titulo: Fundamentally misunderstanding visual perception. Adults' belief in visual emissions (The American Psychologist, 2002, via Europe PMC)
fontes.trecho: Department of Psychology, Ohio State University [...] The authors reviewed research about a profound misconception that is present among college students, namely, the belief that the process of vision includes emanations from the eyes, an idea that is consistent with the extramission theory of perception, which was originally professed by early Greek philosophers and which persisted in scholarly circles for centuries. The authors document the strength and breadth of this phenomenon and the object failure of traditional educational techniques to overcome this belief, and they reveal that students are leaving psychology courses with a flawed understanding of one of the most studied processes in the history of psychology--visual perception.

fontes.titulo: Testing different interpretations for the mistaken belief that rays exit the eyes during vision (The Journal of Psychology, 2003, via Europe PMC)
fontes.trecho: Research has shown that children and adults believe that emissions from the eye occur during the act of vision. [...] supported the hypothesis that extramission notions stem from the outer-oriented phenomenology of vision.

gancho: Para derrubar a ideia de que a luz é uma onda, Poisson calculou que ela previa algo absurdo: um ponto brilhante bem no meio da sombra de um disco. Arago fez o teste, e o ponto estava lá.
explicacao: No começo do século XIX, muitos cientistas preferiam a teoria de Newton, para quem a luz era feita de partículas. Entre eles estava o matemático Siméon Denis Poisson. Em 1818, a Academia de Ciências da França abriu um concurso para explicar as propriedades da luz, e Poisson fazia parte da comissão julgadora. O engenheiro Augustin-Jean Fresnel inscreveu uma nova teoria ondulatória. Poisson a estudou a fundo procurando uma falha e achou o que lhe pareceu uma: pela matemática de Fresnel, a sombra de um objeto circular teria um ponto claro no centro, justamente onde a teoria das partículas previa escuridão total. A previsão soou absurda. Mas o presidente da comissão, François Arago, resolveu fazer o experimento: grudou com cera um disco metálico de 2 milímetros numa placa de vidro e, em 1819, viu o ponto previsto. A explicação é simples: a luz que contorna a borda do disco percorre exatamente a mesma distância até o centro da sombra, chega em fase e se reforça. O teste virou um experimento decisivo a favor das ondas, e o fenômeno ganhou o nome de "ponto de Poisson" ou "ponto de Arago". Arago notou depois que outros dois cientistas já o tinham visto um século antes.

fontes.trecho: In optics, the Arago spot, Poisson spot, or Fresnel spot is a bright point that appears at the center of a circular object's shadow due to Fresnel diffraction. [...] The light coming from points on the circumference of the obstacle and going to the center of the shadow travels exactly the same distance, so all the light passing close by the object arrives at the screen in phase and constructively interferes. This results in a bright spot at the shadow's center, where geometrical optics and particle theories of light predict that there should be no light at all. [...] was the deciding experiment on the question of whether light is a particle or a wave. It is thus an example of an experimentum crucis. At that time, many favored Isaac Newton's corpuscular theory of light, among them the theoretician Siméon Denis Poisson. In 1818 the French Academy of Sciences launched a competition to explain the properties of light, where Poisson was one of the members of the judging committee. The civil engineer Augustin-Jean Fresnel entered this competition by submitting a new wave theory of light. Poisson studied Fresnel's theory in detail and, being a supporter of the particle theory of light, looked for a way to prove it wrong. Poisson thought that he had found a flaw when he argued that a consequence of Fresnel's theory was that there would exist an on-axis bright spot in the shadow of a circular obstacle, where there should be complete darkness according to the particle theory of light. This prediction was seen as an absurd consequence of the wave theory [...] However, the head of the committee, François Arago, decided to actually perform the experiment. He molded a 2 mm metallic disk to a glass plate with wax. He succeeded in observing the predicted spot, confirming Fresnel's prediction in 1819. Arago later noted that the phenomenon (later known as "Poisson's spot" or the "spot of Arago") had already been observed by Joseph-Nicolas Delisle and by Giacomo F. Maraldi a century earlier.

gancho: Em 1676, um astrônomo dinamarquês mostrou que a luz não chega instantaneamente cronometrando os eclipses de uma lua de Júpiter. Ele previu que um desses eclipses viria uns dez minutos atrasado.
explicacao: Ole Rømer trabalhava no Observatório de Paris, onde os eclipses de Io, a mais interna das quatro grandes luas de Júpiter descobertas por Galileu, eram cronometrados com cuidado: Galileu tinha proposto usá-los como um relógio cósmico para calcular a longitude. Rømer notou que o intervalo entre os eclipses não era constante. Quando a Terra e Júpiter estavam se afastando, o intervalo aumentava; quando se aproximavam, diminuía. Como não havia motivo para a órbita de Io mudar, ele concluiu que a diferença vinha do tempo que a luz levava para cruzar uma distância maior ou menor. Pelas contas dele, a luz levaria cerca de 22 minutos para atravessar o diâmetro da órbita da Terra. Aplicadas às órbitas conhecidas hoje, essas contas dão uma velocidade 24,4% abaixo da real. Rømer anunciou que a reaparição de Io em 16 de novembro de 1676 seria vista uns dez minutos depois do que indicava o método antigo. O diretor do observatório, Giovanni Domenico Cassini, nunca aceitou totalmente a ideia, mas Christiaan Huygens e Isaac Newton logo a apoiaram. A confirmação definitiva só veio em 1729, quase duas décadas depois da morte de Rømer, quando James Bradley explicou a aberração estelar. A maior parte dos papéis de Rømer se perdeu no incêndio de Copenhague de 1728.

fontes.titulo: Rømer's determination of the speed of light
fontes.trecho: In 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer demonstrated that light has a measurable speed and so does not travel instantaneously. Rømer was working at the Royal Observatory in Paris at the time. By timing the eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io, Rømer estimated that light would take about 22 minutes to travel a distance equal to the diameter of Earth's orbit around the Sun. Using modern orbits, this would imply a speed of light of 226,663 kilometres per second, 24.4% lower than the true value of 299,792 km/s. [...] Rømer's theory was controversial at the time that he announced it and he never convinced the director of the Paris Observatory, Giovanni Domenico Cassini, to fully accept it. However, it quickly gained support among other natural philosophers of the period such as Christiaan Huygens and Isaac Newton. It was finally confirmed nearly two decades after Rømer's death, with the explanation in 1729 of stellar aberration by the English astronomer James Bradley. [...] Galileo proposed a method of establishing the time of day, and thus longitude, based on the times of the eclipses of the moons of Jupiter, in essence using the Jovian system as a cosmic clock [...] Io is the innermost of the four moons of Jupiter discovered by Galileo in January 1610. [...] The key phenomenon that Rømer observed was that the time between eclipses was not constant, but varied slightly over the year. He was fairly confident that the orbital period of Io was not actually changing, so he deduced that change was a consequence of changes in the distance between Earth and Jupiter. [...] during periods in which Earth and Jupiter were moving away from each other the interval between eclipses always increased, whereas when Earth and Jupiter were moving toward each other, the interval between eclipses decreased. [...] Most of Rømer's papers were destroyed in the Copenhagen Fire of 1728 [...] Most importantly, Rømer announced the prediction that the emergence of Io on 16 November 1676 would be observed about ten minutes later than would have been calculated by the previous method.

gancho: Em 1999, uma equipe de Harvard freou um feixe de luz a cerca de 17 metros por segundo, e em 2001 sua líder conseguiu pará-lo por completo. Antes, ela tivera verba negada por ser teórica.
explicacao: A física dinamarquesa Lene Vestergaard Hau foi formada em física teórica, mas se interessou por um experimento difícil: criar um condensado de Bose-Einstein, um estado especial da matéria. Segundo um relato sobre sua carreira, ela pediu verba à Fundação Nacional de Ciência dos Estados Unidos e ouviu um não, porque uma teórica acharia esse tipo de experimento difícil demais. Hau conseguiu dinheiro em outro lugar e entrou no pequeno grupo de físicos que tinham produzido um condensado. Com ele, sua equipe em Harvard reduziu a velocidade de um feixe de luz para cerca de 17 metros por segundo, num trabalho publicado na revista Nature em 1999. O que é freado é a chamada velocidade de grupo, a do pulso de luz dentro do meio, graças a uma técnica conhecida como transparência induzida eletromagneticamente. Em 2001, Hau foi além e parou um feixe por completo, e depois desenvolveu métodos para pará-lo e soltá-lo de novo. Trabalhos seguintes transferiram a informação da luz para a matéria e de volta para a luz, o que interessa à criptografia e à computação quânticas. Em 2004, pesquisadores de Berkeley conseguiram luz lenta também num semicondutor, a 9,6 quilômetros por segundo.

fontes.trecho: In 1999, she led a Harvard University team that, by use of a Bose–Einstein condensate, succeeded in slowing a beam of light to about 17 metres per second, and, in 2001, was able to stop a beam completely. Later work based on these experiments led to the transfer of light to matter, then from matter back into light, a process with important implications for quantum encryption and quantum computing. [...] Her formalized training is in theoretical physics, but her interest moved to experimental research in an effort to create a new form of matter known as a Bose–Einstein condensate. "Hau applied to the National Science Foundation for funds to make a batch of this condensate but was rejected on the grounds that she was a theorist for whom such experiments would be too difficult to do." Undeterred, she gained alternative funding and became one of the first handful of physicists to create such a condensate.

Group velocities below the speed of light in vacuum c were known to be possible as far back as 1880, but could not be realized in a useful manner until 1991, when Stephen Harris and collaborators demonstrated electromagnetically induced transparency in trapped strontium atoms. [...] Danish physicist Lene Vestergaard Hau led a combined team from Harvard University and the Rowland Institute for Science which realized much lower group velocities of light. They succeeded in slowing a beam of light to about 17 meters per second. In 2004, researchers at UC Berkeley first demonstrated slow light in a semiconductor, with a group velocity 9.6 kilometers per second. Hau and her colleagues later succeeded in stopping light completely, and developed methods by which it can be stopped and later restarted. [...] Lene Vestergaard Hau, S.E. Harris, Zachary Dutton, Cyrus H. Behroozi, Nature v.397, p. 594 (1999).

gancho: O brilho azul da água em volta de reatores nucleares vem de partículas mais rápidas que a luz. Não no vácuo, mas na água, onde a luz anda mais devagar: é como um estrondo sônico, só que de luz.
explicacao: É a radiação Cherenkov. Ela surge quando uma partícula com carga elétrica, como um elétron, atravessa um meio como a água destilada mais depressa do que a luz se propaga nesse meio. A causa lembra a do estrondo sônico, o estalo de um avião que passa a velocidade do som. Marie Curie viu uma luz azul pálida numa solução concentrada de rádio em 1910, mas não investigou a origem. Quem a detectou em experimentos foi o soviético Pavel Cherenkov, em 1934, sob orientação de Sergey Vavilov; ele concluiu que não se tratava de fluorescência. Em 1937, Igor Tamm e Ilya Frank explicaram o efeito com a relatividade especial, e os três dividiram o Nobel de 1958. A emissão é mais forte nas frequências altas, e a maior parte dela cai no ultravioleta; o que sobra visível aparece como um azul brilhante. O efeito também pode acontecer dentro do olho. Por décadas, pacientes em radioterapia contra tumores cerebrais relataram "clarões de luz forte ou azul". Em 2019, pesquisadores de Dartmouth, nos Estados Unidos, registraram com uma câmera especial a luz Cherenkov gerada no humor vítreo desses pacientes.

fontes.trecho: is electromagnetic radiation emitted when a charged particle (such as an electron) passes through a dielectric medium (such as distilled water) at a speed greater than the phase velocity (speed of propagation of a wavefront in a medium) of light in that medium.  A classic example of Cherenkov radiation is the characteristic blue glow of an underwater nuclear reactor. Its cause is similar to the cause of a sonic boom, the sharp sound heard when faster-than-sound movement occurs. [...] The radiation is named after the Soviet scientist Pavel Cherenkov, the 1958 Nobel Prize winner, who was the first to detect it experimentally under the supervision of Sergey Vavilov at the Lebedev Institute in 1934. [...] He discovered the anisotropy of the radiation and came to the conclusion that the bluish glow was not a fluorescent phenomenon. A theory of this effect was later developed in 1937 within the framework of Einstein's special relativity theory by Cherenkov's colleagues Igor Tamm and Ilya Frank, who also shared the 1958 Nobel Prize. [...] Marie Curie observed a pale blue light in a highly concentrated radium solution in 1910, but did not investigate its source. [...] In 2019, a team of researchers from Dartmouth's and Dartmouth-Hitchcock's Norris Cotton Cancer Center discovered Cherenkov light being generated in the vitreous humor of patients undergoing radiotherapy. The light was observed using a camera imaging system called a CDose, which is specially designed to view light emissions from biological systems. For decades, patients had reported phenomena such as "flashes of bright or blue light" when receiving radiation treatments for brain cancer, but the effects had never been experimentally observed. [...] with higher frequencies (shorter wavelengths) being more intense in Cherenkov radiation. Visible Cherenkov radiation is observed to be brilliant blue because while most Cherenkov radiation is in the ultraviolet spectrum

gancho: Desenrolar fita adesiva no vácuo emite raios X, com intensidade suficiente para fazer radiografias. É parente de um efeito que Francis Bacon já notava em 1620: açúcar duro solta faíscas quando quebrado no escuro.
explicacao: O fenômeno se chama triboluminescência: luz que aparece quando um material é rasgado, arranhado, esmagado ou esfregado. Em 1620, no livro Novum Organum, Francis Bacon registrou que todo açúcar duro cintila ao ser quebrado ou raspado no escuro. No fim do século XVIII, quando o açúcar refinado era vendido em grandes cones que precisavam ser partidos, as pessoas viam pequenos clarões ao quebrá-lo com pouca luz. A explicação aceita é que, ao se partir, certos cristais separam cargas elétricas; quando elas se reencontram, a descarga ioniza o ar e produz o clarão, mas o efeito ainda não é totalmente compreendido. As balas de gaultéria funcionam especialmente bem, porque o óleo que as aromatiza converte em azul a luz ultravioleta da descarga. A fita adesiva comum também brilha numa linha no ponto em que descola do rolo. Em 1953, cientistas soviéticos notaram que, no vácuo, ela emitia raios X. Em 2008, um estudo na revista Nature mediu pulsos de raios X de nanossegundos, com 100 miliwatts, sincronizados com os trancos da fita ao descolar, e os autores usaram essa radiação como fonte para fazer imagens de raios X.

fontes.trecho: Triboluminescence is a phenomenon in which light is generated when a material is mechanically pulled apart, ripped, scratched, crushed, or rubbed (see tribology). The phenomenon is not fully understood but appears in most cases to be caused by the separation and reunification of static electric charges [...] The first recorded observation is attributed to English scholar Francis Bacon when he recorded in his 1620 Novum Organum that "It is well known that all sugar, whether candied or plain, if it be hard, will sparkle when broken or scraped in the dark." [...] In the late 1790s, sugar production began to produce more refined sugar crystals. These crystals were formed into a large solid cone for transport and sale. This solid sugar cone had to be broken into usable chunks using a sugar nips device. People began to notice that tiny bursts of light were visible as sugar was "nipped" in low light [...] There remain a few ambiguities about the effect. [...] upon fracture of asymmetrical materials, charge is separated. When the charges recombine, the electrical discharge ionizes the surrounding air, causing a flash of light. [...] Ordinary pressure-sensitive tape ("Scotch tape") displays a glowing line where the end of the tape is being pulled away from the roll. Soviet scientists observed in 1953 that unpeeling a roll of tape in a vacuum produced X-rays.  The mechanism of X-ray generation was studied further in 2008. [...] Wint-O-Green Life Savers work especially well for creating such sparks, because wintergreen oil (methyl salicylate) is fluorescent and converts ultraviolet light into blue light.

fontes.titulo: Correlation between nanosecond X-ray flashes and stick–slip friction in peeling tape (Nature, 2008)
fontes.trecho: Here we report that peeling common adhesive tape in a moderate vacuum produces radio and visible emission3,4, along with nanosecond, 100-mW X-ray pulses that are correlated with stick–slip peeling events. [...] The intensity of X-ray triboluminescence allowed us to use it as a source for X-ray imaging.

gancho: O "moinho de luz", a ampola com pás que giram ao sol, não é movido pela pressão da luz, como dizem até folhetos que vêm com ele. Se fosse, giraria ao contrário. Quem empurra as pás é o pouco ar lá dentro.
explicacao: O radiômetro foi inventado em 1873 pelo químico William Crookes, que notou que a luz do Sol atrapalhava suas pesagens numa câmara com ar rarefeito. Dentro de uma ampola com vácuo parcial, quatro palhetas leves giram num eixo; cada uma tem um lado claro e outro preto, e o lado preto recua diante da luz. Crookes achou que a força vinha da pressão da própria luz, e James Clerk Maxwell, que tinha previsto essa pressão, a princípio concordou. A explicação continua aparecendo em folhetos que acompanham o aparelho, mas não se sustenta. Em 1876, Arthur Schuster mostrou que a ampola sofria uma força no sentido oposto ao das palhetas, sinal de que o empurrão nascia lá dentro. Em 1901, com uma bomba de vácuo melhor, Pyotr Lebedev mostrou que as palhetas ficam paradas num vácuo forte: o aparelho só funciona com um pouco de gás. E a pressão da luz empurraria mais o lado claro, que reflete, do que o preto, que absorve: o giro seria ao contrário. Na verdade, o radiômetro é uma máquina térmica. O lado preto esquenta mais que o claro, e o gás rarefeito, ao contornar as bordas das palhetas, flui do lado frio para o quente, um efeito chamado transpiração térmica, proposto por Osborne Reynolds. Isso aumenta a pressão do lado preto e empurra a palheta. Tanto que, se a parte de fora da ampola for resfriada depressa, as palhetas giram ao contrário.

fontes.trecho: Today the device is mainly used in physics education as a demonstration of a heat engine run by light energy. It was invented in 1873 by the chemist Sir William Crookes as the by-product of some chemical research. In the course of very accurate quantitative chemical work, he was weighing samples in a partially evacuated chamber to reduce the effect of air currents, and noticed the weighings were disturbed when sunlight shone on the balance. [...] Inside the bulb, on a low-friction spindle, is a rotor with several (usually four) vertical lightweight vanes spaced equally around the axis. The vanes are polished or white on one side and black on the other. [...] the dark sides retreating from the radiation source and the light sides advancing. Cooling the outside of the radiometer rapidly causes rotation in the opposite direction. [...] In this case, the black side of the vane becomes hotter than the other side [...] Crookes incorrectly suggested that the force was due to the pressure of light. This theory was originally supported by James Clerk Maxwell, who had predicted this force. This explanation is still often seen in leaflets packaged with the device. The first experiment to test this theory was done by Arthur Schuster in 1876, who observed that there was a force on the glass bulb of the Crookes radiometer that was in the opposite direction to the rotation of the vanes. This showed that the force turning the vanes was generated inside the radiometer. [...] In 1901, with a better vacuum pump, Pyotr Lebedev showed that, in fact, the radiometer only works when there is low-pressure gas in the bulb, and the vanes stay motionless in a hard vacuum. Finally, if light pressure were the motive force, the radiometer would spin in the opposite direction, as the photons on the shiny side being reflected would deposit more momentum than on the black side, where the photons are absorbed. [...] The currently accepted theory was formulated by Osborne Reynolds, who theorized that thermal transpiration was the cause of the motion. [...] As gas moves from the cooler to the hotter side, the pressure on the hotter side increases.

gancho: Em 1800, Herschel pôs um termômetro além do vermelho do espectro e achou uma luz invisível que esquenta: o infravermelho. Um ano depois, Ritter buscou além do violeta um raio que esfriasse e achou o ultravioleta.
explicacao: William Herschel, o astrônomo, usou um prisma para abrir a luz do Sol em cores e percebeu que o termômetro subia na região escura logo depois do vermelho. Surpreso, chamou aquilo de "raios caloríficos" e apresentou o resultado à Royal Society de Londres em 1800. O nome "infravermelho", do latim "infra", abaixo, só surgiu no fim do século XIX. Os estudos que se seguiram mostraram que um pouco mais da metade da energia do Sol que chega à Terra vem nessa forma. No ano seguinte, o alemão Johann Wilhelm Ritter, influenciado pela filosofia romântica que buscava polaridades na natureza, decidiu procurar no outro extremo do espectro um raio oposto, que esfriasse. Não achou o que esperava. Mas notou que o cloreto de prata, que escurece com a luz, ficava preto mais depressa na região escura além do violeta do que sob o próprio violeta. Ele chamou esses raios de "desoxidantes", para destacar sua ação química; depois ficaram conhecidos como "raios químicos" e, por fim, ultravioleta. Ritter nunca teve renda fixa nem chegou a professor universitário.

fontes.trecho: In 1800 the astronomer Sir William Herschel discovered that infrared radiation is a type of invisible radiation in the spectrum lower in energy than red light, by means of its effect on a thermometer. Slightly more than half of the energy from the Sun was eventually found, through Herschel's studies, to arrive on Earth in the form of infrared. [...] Herschel published his results in 1800 before the Royal Society of London. Herschel used a prism to refract light from the sun and detected the infrared, beyond the red part of the spectrum, through an increase in the temperature recorded on a thermometer. He was surprised at the result and called them "Calorific Rays". The term "infrared" did not appear until the late 19th century. The Latin prefix infra- means below

UV radiation was discovered in February 1801 when the German physicist Johann Wilhelm Ritter observed that invisible rays just beyond the violet end of the visible spectrum darkened silver chloride-soaked paper more quickly than violet light itself. He announced the discovery in a very brief letter to the Annalen der Physik and later called them "(de-)oxidizing rays" (German: de-oxidierende Strahlen) to emphasize chemical reactivity and to distinguish them from "heat rays", discovered the previous year at the other end of the visible spectrum. The simpler term "chemical rays" was adopt

He is associated with the German Romanticism. [...] Many of Ritter's researches were guided by a search for polarities in the several "forces" of nature [...] In 1801, after hearing about the discovery of "heat rays" (infrared radiation) by William Herschel (in 1800), Ritter looked for an opposite (cooling) radiation at the other end of the visible spectrum. He did not find exactly what he expected to find, but after a series of attempts he noticed that silver chloride was transformed faster from white to black when it was placed at the dark region of the Sun's spectrum, close to its violet end. The "chemical rays" found by him were afterwards called ultraviolet radiation. [...] Ritter had no regular income and never became a university professor

gancho: Em 1861, Maxwell exibiu a primeira foto colorida pelo método das três cores: uma fita listrada, com vermelho. Um século depois, notou-se o enigma: o material fotográfico usado era praticamente cego ao vermelho.
explicacao: Em 1855, num trabalho sobre a visão das cores, o físico escocês James Clerk Maxwell propôs o método que ainda é a base da maioria dos processos coloridos, químicos ou eletrônicos. Com um disco giratório, ele mostrara que qualquer tom pode ser obtido misturando só três luzes: vermelha, verde e azul. A ideia era tirar três fotos em preto e branco da mesma cena, cada uma através de um filtro dessas cores, e depois projetá-las sobrepostas, cada uma com o seu filtro. Em 1861, o fotógrafo Thomas Sutton fez as três imagens de um laço de fita listrada para uma palestra de Maxwell sobre cores, que tratava de física e fisiologia, não de fotografia. O próprio Maxwell achou o resultado fraco e disse que faltava um material mais sensível ao vermelho e ao verde. Cem anos depois, os historiadores estranharam que aparecesse qualquer vermelho: o processo de Sutton era, na prática, insensível a essa cor, e pouco sensível ao verde. A resposta veio em 1961. Muitos corantes vermelhos também refletem ultravioleta, e o filtro vermelho de Sutton, por coincidência, deixava passar essa luz. As três imagens provavelmente registraram ultravioleta, azul-esverdeado e azul, e não vermelho, verde e azul.

fontes.trecho: The three-color method, the foundation of most color processes, chemical or electronic, was first suggested in an 1855 paper on color vision by Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell. [...] In his studies of color vision, Maxwell showed, by using a rotating disk with which he could alter the proportions, that any visible hue or gray tone could be made by mixing only three pure colors of light – red, green and blue [...] if three colorless photographs of the same scene were taken through red, green and blue filters, and transparencies ("slides") made from them were projected through the same filters and superimposed on a screen, the result would be an image reproducing not only red, green and blue, but all of the colors in the original scene. [...] The first color photograph made according to Maxwell's prescription, a set of three monochrome "color separations", was taken by Thomas Sutton in 1861 for use in illustrating a lecture on color by Maxwell, where it was shown in color by the triple projection method. [...] The test subject was a bow made of ribbon with stripes of various colors, apparently including red and green. [...] During the lecture, which was about physics and physiology, not photography, Maxwell commented on the inadequacy of the results and the need for a photographic material more sensitive to red and green light. [...] A century later, historians were mystified by the reproduction of any red at all, because the photographic process used by Sutton was for all practical purposes totally insensitive to red light and only marginally sensitive to green. [...] In 1961, researchers found that many red dyes also reflect ultraviolet light, coincidentally transmitted by Sutton's red filter, and surmised that the three images were probably due to ultra-violet, blue-green and blue wavelengths, rather than to red, green and blue.

gancho: Sem LED azul não havia lâmpada de LED branca, e ele resistiu aos cientistas por três décadas. Um dos japoneses que o criaram diz ter ganhado só 20 mil ienes da empresa pela invenção. Processou e levou 840 milhões.
explicacao: Diodos vermelhos e verdes existiam havia muito tempo, mas, sem o azul, não dava para fazer lâmpadas brancas, e o LED azul desafiou a ciência e a indústria por três décadas. Shuji Nakamura trabalhava na Nichia, uma pequena empresa de Tokushima, num projeto com nitreto de gálio que muitos achavam inviável. Depois que o fundador passou a presidência ao genro, em 1989, a direção mandou suspender a pesquisa por gastar tempo e dinheiro demais. Nakamura continuou por conta própria e, em 1993, chegou a um LED azul mil vezes mais brilhante que os anteriores. Coberta por um material que converte parte da luz azul em amarela, essa luz vira branca: é a base das lâmpadas de LED. As receitas da Nichia passaram de cerca de 20 bilhões de ienes em 1993 para 80 bilhões em 2001, 60% deles vindos do LED azul. Nakamura afirma ter recebido só 20 mil ienes pela patente; a empresa diz que o compensou com promoções e bônus. Em 2001 ele a processou, e um tribunal chegou a lhe conceder 20 bilhões de ienes. Após recurso, o acordo de 2005 ficou em 840 milhões, ainda assim o maior já pago por uma empresa japonesa a um funcionário por uma invenção. Em 2014, ele dividiu o Nobel de Física com Isamu Akasaki e Hiroshi Amano.

fontes.trecho: co-inventor of the blue LED, a major breakthrough in lighting technology. For this achievement, Nakamura, together with Isamu Akasaki and Hiroshi Amano, received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2014. [...] It was while working for Nichia that Nakamura invented the method for producing the first commercial high brightness gallium nitride (GaN) LED whose brilliant blue light, when partially converted to yellow by a phosphor coating, is the key to white LED lighting [...] At the time, many considered creating a GaN LED too difficult to produce [...] However, the senior Ogawa ceded the presidency to his son-in-law Eiji Ogawa (in 1989). The company under Eiji's direction ordered him to suspend work on GaN, claiming it was consuming too much time and money. Nakamura continued to develop the blue LED on his own and in 1993 succeeded in making the device. Despite these circumstances, once Nakamura succeeded in creating a commercially viable prototype, 3 orders of magnitude (1000 times) brighter than previously successful blue LEDs [...] The company's gross receipt surged from just over ¥20 billion (≈US$200 million) in 1993 to ¥80 billion (≈US$800 million) by 2001, 60 percent of which was accounted for by sales of blue LED products. [...] In 2001, Nakamura sued his former employer Nichia over his bonus for the discovery [...] Nakamura claimed that he received only ¥20,000 (≈US$180) for his discovery of "404 patent," [...] opined that the company had adequately compensated him for the innovation through promotions and bonuses [...] Nakamura sued for ¥2 billion (<US$20 million) as his fair share for the invention, and the district court awarded him ten times the amount, ¥20 billion (<US$200 million). However, Nichia appealed the award and the parties settled in 2005 for ¥840 million (≈US$8.1 million, less than 5% of the award amount), which was still the largest payment ever paid by a Japanese company to an employee for an invention

fontes.titulo: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2014 – Press release (NobelPrize.org)
fontes.trecho: Red and green diodes had been around for a long time but without blue light, white lamps could not be created. Despite considerable efforts, both in the scientific community and in industry, the blue LED had remained a challenge for three decades. [...] Nakamura was employed at Nichia Chemicals, a small company in Tokushima.

gancho: A água é azul por conta própria, e não só porque reflete o céu: suas moléculas vibram e absorvem um pouco do vermelho. Um lago de água pesada, feita com um hidrogênio mais pesado, não teria esse azul.
explicacao: Num copo, a água parece incolor, mas a água pura tem um leve tom azul que se aprofunda com a espessura. Dá para ver olhando uma luz branca através de um tubo de um metro ou mais cheio de água purificada. Em geral, as cores das coisas vêm de elétrons absorvendo luz, mas na água essas absorções caem todas no ultravioleta. O azul vem de outro lugar: das vibrações da molécula. As ligações entre oxigênio e hidrogênio vibram em frequências do infravermelho, e uma combinação de harmônicos dessas vibrações chega à borda do vermelho: na água líquida a 20 °C, absorve em torno de 740 e 660 nanômetros. A absorção é fraca, por isso só aparece em grandes volumes. Na água pesada, em que o hidrogênio é trocado pelo deutério, as vibrações têm menos energia e se deslocam para o infravermelho; ela não absorve o vermelho, e uma grande massa dela não teria o azul da água comum. Achar que mares e lagos são azuis só por refletirem o céu é um equívoco comum: piscinas cobertas, com fundo branco, também ficam azuladas, e mais ainda quanto mais fundas. As partículas em suspensão também importam: sem elas para espalhar a luz de volta, algumas dezenas de metros de água absorveriam tudo, e o mar pareceria preto.

fontes.trecho: While relatively small quantities of water appear to be colorless and transparent, pure water has a slight blue color that becomes deeper as the thickness of the observed sample increases. [...] The intrinsic color of liquid water may be demonstrated by looking at a white light source through a long pipe that is filled with purified water and closed at both ends with a transparent window. The light sky blue color is caused by weak absorption in the red part of the visible spectrum. Absorptions in the visible spectrum are usually attributed to excitations of electronic energy states in matter. Water is a simple three-atom molecule, H2O, and all its electronic absorptions occur in the ultraviolet region of the electromagnetic spectrum and are therefore not responsible for the color of water in the visible region of the spectrum. [...] Two stretching vibrations of the O–H bonds in the gaseous state of water occur at [...] Absorption due to these vibrations occurs in the infrared region of the spectrum. [...] In liquid state at 20 °C (68 °F) these vibrations are red-shifted by hydrogen bonding, resulting in red absorption at 740 nm, other harmonics such as v1 + v2 + 3v3 giving red absorption at 660 nm. The absorption curve for heavy water (D2O) is of a similar shape, but is shifted further towards the infrared end of the spectrum, because the vibrational transitions have a lower energy. For this reason, heavy water does not absorb red light and thus large bodies of D2O would lack the characteristic sky blue of the more commonly found light water (1H2O). [...] the pipe needs to have a length of a meter or more and the water must be purified [...] It is a common misconception that this reflection is the sole reason bodies of water appear cyan, though it can contribute. [...] Water in swimming pools with white-painted sides and bottom will appear cyan, even in indoor pools where there is no sky to be reflected. The deeper the pool, the more intense the cyan color becomes. [...] A few tens of meters of water will absorb all light, so without scattering, all bodies of water would appear black.

gancho: Muita gente consegue perceber a polarização da luz a olho nu. Ela aparece como uma "gravatinha" amarelada e fraca no centro da visão, ao olhar o céu azul ou uma tela branca de LCD inclinando a cabeça.
explicacao: O fenômeno se chama pincel de Haidinger, em homenagem ao físico austríaco Wilhelm Karl von Haidinger, que o descreveu em 1844 depois de vê-lo ao olhar através de minerais que polarizam a luz. A figura é uma barra amarelada, ou um laço de gravata, com as pontas borradas, que ocupa de 3 a 5 graus do campo visual: duas ou três vezes a largura do polegar com o braço esticado. Entre as partes amarelas pode haver áreas azuladas ou arroxeadas, ainda mais fracas. A barra fica perpendicular à direção em que a luz está polarizada e some em poucos segundos, porque o sistema nervoso se adapta, a menos que a pessoa gire os olhos ou incline a cabeça. A causa costuma ser atribuída a um pigmento amarelo da mácula, a região central da retina, cujas moléculas absorvem a luz de modo diferente conforme a polarização; o tamanho do pincel bate com o da mácula. Para vê-lo, o mais fácil é girar a lente de um óculos de sol polarizado diante de uma superfície clara e lisa. No céu, a polarização é mais forte a 90 graus do Sol. O efeito tem até uso clínico: ajuda a treinar pessoas com certos tipos de estrabismo a voltar a fixar o olhar com o centro da retina.

fontes.trecho: an entoptic phenomenon, first described by Austrian physicist Wilhelm Karl von Haidinger in 1844. Haidinger saw it when he looked through various minerals that polarized light. Many people are able to perceive polarization of light. Haidinger's brushes may be seen as a yellowish horizontal bar or bow-tie shape (with "fuzzy" ends, hence the name "brush") visible in the center of the visual field against the blue sky viewed while facing approximately 90° from the sun, or on any bright background. Haidinger's yellow bar is observed perpendicular to the direction of light polarization [...] The perception of this effect vanishes within a few seconds due to neural adaptation unless the observer rotates the eyes (like by moving the head sideways). It typically occupies roughly 3–5 degrees of vision, about twice or three times the width of one's thumb held at arm's length. Fainter bluish or purplish areas may be visible between the yellow brushes (see illustration).  Haidinger's brush may also be seen by looking at a white area on many LCD flat panel computer screens (due to the polarization effect of the display) [...] Haidinger's brush is usually attributed to the dichroism of the xanthophyll pigment found in the macula lutea. [...] The size of the brush is consistent with the size of the macula. [...] To see Haidinger's brush, start by using a polarizer, such as a lens from a pair of polarizing sunglasses. Gaze at an evenly lit, textureless surface through the lens and rotate the polarizer. [...] The areas of the sky with the strongest polarization are those 90 degrees away from the sun. [...] People with certain types of strabismus may undergo an adaptation whereupon they look at the object of attention not with their fovea (at the centre of the macula) but with an eccentric region of the retina. [...] To aid in training a person to look at an object with their fovea rather than their eccentric retinal zone, a training device can be used.

gancho: Se toda a luz do universo fosse misturada, que cor daria? Astrônomos fizeram a conta com mais de 200 mil galáxias: um branco puxado para o bege. Batizaram de "cosmic latte" e se disseram "tendenciosos à cafeína".
explicacao: Em 2002, Karl Glazebrook e Ivan Baldry, da Universidade Johns Hopkins, somaram os espectros de mais de 200 mil galáxias de um grande levantamento do céu e montaram o "espectro cósmico", toda a luz das estrelas num grande volume do universo. A cor não era o objetivo: as linhas escuras do espectro revelam a proporção de estrelas jovens e velhas e, com isso, a história da formação estelar. O resultado indica que a maioria das estrelas atuais se formou há mais de 5 bilhões de anos e que o universo já foi mais azul, quando havia mais estrelas jovens e quentes, e vai ficando mais vermelho. Primeiro, a dupla anunciou um verde esbranquiçado, mas logo corrigiu a análise para um bege esbranquiçado. A cor é tão próxima do branco que um erro pequeno teve efeito grande, e ela depende do que o olho toma como branco: sob lâmpadas incandescentes, a mesma luz pareceria bem azul. Os pesquisadores pediram sugestões de nome, aceitando qualquer uma que não fosse "bege". "Cappuccino cosmico" teve mais votos, mas eles ficaram com "cosmic latte": "latte" é "leite" em italiano, a língua de Galileu, e lembra a Via Láctea, "Via Lattea".

fontes.trecho: Cosmic latte is the average color of the galaxies of the universe as perceived by a typical human observer from the position of the Earth. In 2002, astronomers Karl Glazebrook and Ivan Baldry from Johns Hopkins University determined that the average color of the universe was a whiteish green. Still, they soon corrected their analysis in a 2003 paper in which they reported that their survey of the light from over 200,000 galaxies averaged to a whiteish beige. [...] Finding the average color of the universe was not the focus of the study. Rather, the study examined spectral analysis of different galaxies to study star formation. [...] jokingly adding all were welcome as long as they were not "beige". [...] Though Drum's suggestion of "cappuccino cosmico" received the most votes, the researchers favored Drum's other suggestion, "cosmic latte". "Latte" means "milk" in Italian, Galileo's native language, and the similar "latteo" means "milky", similar to the Italian term for the Milky Way, "Via Lattea". [...] They also claimed to be "caffeine biased".

fontes.titulo: The Cosmic Spectrum and the Color of the Universe – Karl Glazebrook & Ivan Baldry (Johns Hopkins University, arquivado)
fontes.trecho: a new survey of more than 200,000 galaxies which measures the light from a large volume of the Universe [...] This is constructed by adding together all the individual spectra of the separate galaxies in the 2dF survey. [...] However if one were to introduce a beam of cosmic spectrum into a room strongly illuminated by light bulbs only (Illuminant A) it would appear very blue [...] Really the answer is so close to white, it is difficult to say. That is why such a small error had such a large effect. [...] all of them say that the majority of stars in the Universe today formed more than 5 billion years ago. This of course implies that the color of the Universe would have been different in the past when there were more hot young blue stars. [...] The universe started out young and blue, and grew gradually redder as the population of evolved 'red' giant stars built up.

gancho: A lei da refração, que diz como a luz se desvia ao passar do ar para a água ou o vidro, leva o nome do holandês Snell, de 1621. Mas já aparece num tratado escrito em Bagdá por volta de 984, sobre lentes que queimam.
explicacao: Ptolomeu, em Alexandria, já tinha proposto uma relação entre os ângulos da luz que entra e da que se desvia, mas ela falhava para ângulos maiores; Ptolomeu se convenceu de que estava certa em parte porque ajustou os dados para caberem na teoria. A forma correta aparece no tratado "Sobre os instrumentos que queimam", escrito por volta de 984 por Ibn Sahl, matemático ligado à corte dos buídas em Bagdá. Ele usou a lei para desenhar lentes que concentram a luz sem distorção geométrica, e lentes convexas capazes de pôr fogo num objeto a uma distância definida. O texto foi reconstruído pelo historiador Roshdi Rashed a partir de dois manuscritos, um em Damasco e outro em Teerã. Na Europa, a lei foi redescoberta várias vezes. Thomas Harriot chegou a ela em 1602 e não publicou, embora tenha trocado cartas com Kepler sobre o assunto. Willebrord Snellius, o Snell, deduziu uma forma equivalente em 1621, que também ficou inédita enquanto ele viveu. René Descartes a publicou em 1637, e foi acusado por Isaac Vossius, e depois por Fermat e Huygens, de ter copiado Snell, acusação que hoje se considera injusta. Na França, ela costuma ser chamada de lei de Snell-Descartes.

fontes.trecho: Snell's law (also known as the Snell–Descartes law, and the law of refraction) is a formula used to describe the relationship between the angles of incidence and refraction, when referring to light or other waves passing through a boundary between two different isotropic media, such as water, glass, or air. [...] Ptolemy, in Alexandria, Egypt, had found a relationship regarding refraction angles, but it was inaccurate for angles that were not small. Ptolemy was confident he had found an accurate empirical law, partially as a result of slightly altering data to fit his theory [...] The law was eventually named after Snell, although it was first discovered by the Persian scientist Ibn Sahl, at Baghdad court in 984. In the manuscript On Burning Mirrors and Lenses, Sahl used the law to derive lens shapes that focus light with no geometric aberration. [...] The law was rediscovered by Thomas Harriot in 1602, who however did not publish his results although he had corresponded with Kepler on this very subject. In 1621, the Dutch astronomer Willebrord Snellius (1580–1626)—Snell—derived a mathematically equivalent form, that remained unpublished during his lifetime. René Descartes independently derived the law using heuristic momentum conservation arguments in terms of sines in his 1637 essay La Dioptrique [...] We now know this charge to be undeserved but it has been adopted many times since."  Both Fermat and Huygens repeated this accusation that Descartes had copied Snell. In French, Snell's Law is sometimes called  "la loi de Descartes" or more frequently "loi de Snell-Descartes". [...] In De natura lucis et proprietate (1662) Isaac Vossius said that Descartes had seen Snell's paper and concocted his own proof.

c. 940–1000) was a mathematician and physicist of the Islamic Golden Age, associated with the Buyid court of Baghdad. He is known to have written an optical treatise around 984. The text of this treatise was reconstructed by Roshdi Rashed from two manuscripts (edited 1993).: Damascus [...] and Tehran [...] The Damascus manuscript has the title Fī al-'āla al-muḥriqa "On the burning instruments" [...] Ibn Sahl dealt with the optical properties of curved mirrors and lenses and has been described as the discoverer of the law of refraction (Snell's law). [...] Ibn Sahl designed convex lenses that focus light rays that are parallel, which can cause an object to burn at a specific distance.
